translations.ita: Oggi berrò vino, domani starò senza
translations.eng: Today I will drink wine, tomorrow I will do without

commentary.text: The inscription is commonly interpreted as a popular saying corresponding to a carpe diem exhortation (see, for example, Vetter 1953 and Giacomelli 1963). Alternatively, it has been proposed to interpret it as an invite to drink wine every day (see Rigobianco 2017), as for anyone who reads and interprets the text, it is always today (foied), time to drink, and the abstinence is put off until a tomorrow (cra) which never comes, according to a mechanism which is often used in playful written texts

According to Giacomelli 1963, the alternation between ⟨f⟩ and ⟨h⟩ at the beginning of a word, which is attested in Faliscan words such as foied/hoied, would be due to sociolinguistic factors. Bakkum 2009 has suggested that foied would be a hypercorrected form for hoied (*/hō(d)+di̭ē(d)/) consequent to the the Middle Faliscan change */#fV/ > [#hV]

The verbal forms pipafo and pafo have been largely debated by scholars. Essentially, they have been considered and variously explained as two concomitant forms (see, for example, Giacomelli 1963) or, alternatively, pafo has been interpreted as an error for pipafo (see, for example, Bakkum 2009, Rigobianco 2017 and references therein)
The same text is attested in a Latin inscription, albeit fragmentary, painted on a kylix found in the Palatine (see Ferrandes, Nonnis, and Pola 2021).

According to Garrucci 1864 the inscription pertains to the burial of two woman, respectively Gauia Ueculia and Gauia Egnata Thania; in this case, Thania should be considered as a matronymic. Vetter 1953 argued that the second ca could not be the abbreviation of a woman's name, instead it should be an abbreviation of a man's name like Gauio. Thus, he suggested that the inscription pertains to the burial of a woman (Gauia Ueculia) and her three slaves (Gauio, Egnata, Thania). Later this suggestion was adopted by Giacomelli 1963. A third suggestion was proposed by Bakkum 2009: according to him the burial pertains to three women, respectively Gauia Ueculia, Gauia Egnata and Thania

Later, this suggestion was adopted by Giacomelli 1963. An other suggestion (based on the hypothesis expressed by Herbig 1910 and Rix 1965) was adopted by Bakkum 2009: he argued that olna could be a second gentilicium

Bakkum 2009 argued that these suggestions could not be correct because these form are not attested from the ager Faliscus or Capenas. Vetter 1953 and later Giacomelli 1963 adopted the form [ui]pi. Again Bakkum 2009 argued that this form cannot be considered as correct because it appear to be incompatible with the traces preserved at the beginning of the inscription. According to Bakkum 2009, the inscriptions Ve 264 a-m/Giacomelli 15 I-XII/Bakkum 113-124 may have been produced in series because they are quite identical one to each other and they are painted in identical black-varnished Etrusco-Campanian cups. He suggested that probably they were produced as ready-made ex-votos to be sold at the temple or as dedications imposed by the aediles as sanction

Most editors had underlined the strange juxtaposition between titoi and mercui because titoi was considered as a praenomen (even if it is not used frequently in Faliscan inscriptions). About this topic, Poccetti 2009 undelined that the union between a praenomen/gentilicium and a theonym to identify a deity is a common fact in Italic religious world. He suggested that titoi could be a form that corresponds to the praenomen attested in the Italic onomastics or it could be an epithet that has the same origin of the praenomen. This latter hypothesis has been suggested by Combet-Farnoux 1980 and Bakkum 2009 too. They considered titoi as an adjective with the meaning of 'propitious' or 'prosperous'

Thulin 1907 suggested that mercui could be a dative. Later this suggestion was accepted by most editors eccept Pisani 1933, who thought that this form could be a genitive. In this case the ending -oi might be derived from the development of -osio. Bakkum 2009 didn't accepted this suggestion and, even if he undelined the morphophonological problems about considering -oi as a dative singular ending of the fourth nominal declension, it seems that he adopted this last suggestion. According to him, the ending could be derived analogically from the dative singular ending of the first and second nominal declensions. The name of the deity mercui could be connected to Latin merx and Oscan mirikui (see for example: Vetter 1953; Giacomelli 1963; Bakkum 2009)

efiles has been considered a calque from Latin aedilis (see for example Giacomelli 1963). According to Bakkum 2009 it is not necessary a calque based on Latin aedilis. commentary.text: Both Vetter 1953 and Giacomelli 1963 have adopted the suggestion proposed by Thulin 1907 according to which line 1 and 2 should be considered as pertaining to two different inscriptions, referring to two different burials. Therefore, the tomb whould have been used in different stages for the burial of more than three deceased. Bakkum 2009 has proposed the translation 'the tomb of Gavius Pavicius, Lucius' son' for this inscription, while being aware of the awkward syntax of the inscription. Alternatively, he has suggested that the inscriptions Bakkum 11 and 12 should be divided into 'cauio pauiceo' and 'uolti teti locies cela' but the epigraphical differences between the sequences 'uolti teti' and 'locies cela' makes it difficult to believe that they pertain to the same inscription.

commentary.text: The reading and the interpretation of the inscription are doubtful. We can give some suggestions based on the linguistic and comparative evidences
Q and haloi could be interpreted as a formula composed of a praenomen plus a gentilicium. They could be datives

Teti and atroni could be interpreted as a formula composed of a praenomen plus a gentilicium. They could be considered as abbrevieted nominatives or as genitives. This latter suggestion is less plausible due to syntactic and textual features. Moreover, teti is usually attested as a gentilicium and not as a praenomen

date_text: beginning of the third century BC

commentary.text: The punctuation used in ne.roni is considered as an error by Vetter 1953, Giacomelli 1963, Bakkum 2009

Bakkum 2009 considered neroni as an abbrevieted nominative and didnt't accept the suggestion proposed by Pisani 1964. He suggested that the -i ending of this form could be the result of a language contact with the Etruscan, specifically a number of forms in -i have been interpreted as Etruscan feminine forms. In several cases this is plausible but according to Bakkum 2009 this could not be the case
